newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIA RATE OUTLOOK NO CLEARER AFTER JOBS DATA.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIA RATE OUTLOOK NO CLEARER AFTER JOBS DATA.

text.p: The outlook for Australian interest rates was no clearer after Thursday's release of July labour force data which held something for those looking for another cut and something for those who believe the easing cycle has ended.
Total employment rose by 21,300 in July, close to median expectations of a 25,000 rise, official data showed.
Despite the jobs rise, the unemployment rate moved higher, to 8.7 percent from 8.5 percent in June.
While the data contained some tentative signs of improvement in the stalled job market, analysts cautioned that it would be dangerous to read too much into one month's data.
"I think we need a few more months of strong employment growth before we can shut the book on the weak labour market story," Toronto Dominion chief economist Gavin Stacey said.
The most positive news in the figures for analysts was a 52,500 rise in full-time employment, one area of the labour market that has been particularly weak over the past year.
However, despite the hefty rise, full-time employment levels are still below the level of July last year, and a total of 11,400 full-time jobs have been lost this year, the data showed.

For its part, the government remains optimistic on the labour market. While describing the current state of the market as flat, employment minister Amanda Vanstone said the outlook for jobs was positive heading into the end of 1997.
"The outlook for coming months is positive, however, with the effects of the most recent interest rate cuts yet to be felt," Vanstone said in a statement.

The stagnant labour market has been a key factor in each of the five rate cuts delivered by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) since July 31 last year, the most recent happening last week, and further weakness would have been interpreted by markets as a signal for a possible sixth rate cut.
As it was, Thursday's data did little to change opinions on the likelihood of another cut.

"If you're inclined to think there's another rate cut, you can still argue one out of this and if you're inclined to think there isn't one, you can back up that up that view with the full-time employment rise giving a hint of some improvement to
come," UBS Australia chief economist Stephen Roberts said.

Those who believe the easing cycle has come to an end pointed to rise in full-time employment and said that given the 12 to 18 month lag between rate cuts and stronger growth, the conditions were in place for the labour market to improve.
"Our view is that we have probably seen the worst of the bad labour market news, with employment growth likely to pick up from here," Bankers Trust senior economist David Bassanese said.
Against this, those in facour of a rate cut pointed to continuing high unemployment, and a stagnant labour market that has only created 17,300 jobs over the first seven months of the year.

"Only one of the three volatile components of the labour force was strong," Westpac general manager of economics Bill Evans said of the full-time employment rise, pointing to a large fall in part-time employment and the higher unemployment rate.

When the first cut was delivered last year, the then RBA Governor, Bernie Fraser, noted that an earlier downtrend in the unemployment rate had stalled at around 8.5 percent. Since that first cut, the unemployment rate has not been below 8.5 percent.

"The unemployment rate is really stuck above 8.5 percent and we don't see that coming down in a hurry. The figures still maintain an easing bias to policy," Merrill Lynch Australia chief economist Nigel Douglas said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
